sourceCourseTitle: Ai Governance Compliance Responsible Ai Leader / NIST AI RMF and GenAI Profile

body.en:
**In this lesson you will learn:**

- 1) The purpose and structure of the NIST AI Risk Management Framework (AI RMF) core and crosscutting functions—Govern, Map, Measure, and Manage.
- 2) How trustworthiness characteristics (valid/reliable, safe, secure/resilient, accountable/transparent, explainable/interpretable, privacy-enhanced, and fair with harmful bias managed) translate into requirements and controls.
- 3) Practical artifacts, roles, and processes to operationalize the framework across the AI lifecycle.

blocks.title: How to use the AI Act Single Information Platform
blocks.label: Course Video

body.en:
The NIST AI RMF is a voluntary, risk-based, socio-technical framework to help organizations design, develop, deploy, and use trustworthy AI. It defines a crosscutting Govern function and three lifecycle functions—Map, Measure, and Manage—that work together to identify, assess, and treat AI risk.

Govern establishes leadership, accountability, and policies that enable responsible AI. Map characterizes the AI system and context of use, including stakeholders, intended use/misuse, data, and potential impacts.

Measure develops and executes test, evaluation, verification, and validation (TEVV) to quantify risks (e.g., safety, bias, robustness, privacy). Manage prioritizes risks, implements controls, monitors post-deployment, and conducts incident response and continuous improvement.

The framework emphasizes documentation (risk register, impact assessments, data statements, model/system cards), clear roles, and iterative monitoring to maintain trustworthiness over time.

• Govern (crosscutting): Define roles and accountability, risk appetite, policies, training, documentation standards, and a culture that incentivizes responsible behavior.
• Map + Measure: Map the system’s purpose, context, stakeholders, data lineage, and potential harms; then Measure with TEVV—metrics for efficacy, bias/fairness, robustness, privacy, explainability, and security (including red teaming and uncertainty analysis).
• Manage (treatment + monitoring): Prioritize risks, select and implement controls, plan change management and incident response, monitor in production, and retire/decommission safely.

• Govern sets organization-wide accountability, policies, and culture for AI risk.
• Map, Measure, and Manage work iteratively to identify context, generate evidence, and treat/monitor risks.
• Documentation, clear roles, and continuous monitoring are essential to sustaining trustworthy AI.
Congratulations! You have completed this lesson. You now understand the NIST AI RMF functions and how to apply them across the AI lifecycle.

body.en:
**In this lesson you will learn:**

- 1) The generative AI risk landscape highlighted in NIST AI 600-1 (Generative AI Risk Management Profile).
- 2) How GenAI risks map to the AI RMF functions and what mitigations NIST recommends in practice.
- 3) How to evaluate and monitor GenAI systems for issues like hallucinations, prompt injection, memorization/privacy leakage, harmful content, and misuse.

NIST AI 600-1 tailors the AI RMF to generative AI by profiling common failure modes, impact scenarios, and actionable practices across Govern, Map, Measure, and Manage. GenAI introduces distinctive risks: hallucinations and fabrication, prompt injection and jailbreaks, data leakage and memorization of training data, toxic or biased content, code-generation and tool-use safety issues, misinformation and synthetic media misuse, intellectual property and copyright concerns, and evaluation difficulties under distribution shift.

The profile emphasizes organizational governance (clear use policies, model release and access controls, documentation such as system/model cards), contextual mapping (intended use and misuse, stakeholder harms, data provenance), rigorous measurement (adversarial evaluations, red teaming, toxicity/PII detectors, grounding checks, robustness testing), and risk treatment and monitoring (guardrails, human-in-the-loop review, content filtering, provenance and authenticity measures such as C2PA, cautious use of watermarks with awareness of limitations, sandboxed tool invocation, rate limiting, logging, incident response, and post-deployment monitoring). It highlights secure RAG patterns (treat retrieved content as untrusted, constrain tool actions, and validate outputs) and stresses continuous improvement as models, data, and threats evolve.

body.en:
• Failure modes: Hallucinations, prompt injection/jailbreaks, training-data memorization and privacy leakage, harmful/biased/toxic outputs, misuse of synthetic media, insecure code/agent actions.
• Controls: Policy and access controls, input/output filtering, grounding with citations, secure RAG (isolate untrusted content), tool-use allowlists and sandboxes, rate limiting, provenance/authenticity measures (e.g., C2PA), and careful use of watermarking.
• Evaluation & monitoring: Red teaming with adversarial prompts, scenario-based tests for safety/bias/robustness, detectors for toxicity/PII, canary strings for leakage checks, comprehensive logging and incident response.

• GenAI introduces unique risks such as hallucinations, prompt injection, memorization, and synthetic media misuse.
• NIST AI 600-1 profiles these risks and maps practical mitigations across Govern, Map, Measure, and Manage.
• Secure RAG patterns, robust eval/red teaming, provenance/authenticity, and continuous monitoring are central to reducing GenAI risk.
Congratulations! You have completed this lesson. You can now identify GenAI-specific risks and apply NIST AI 600-1 guidance to manage them effectively.

title.en: Controls and Evidence (NIST AI RMF & GenAI Profile)

body.en:
**In this lesson you will learn:**

- 1) How to design preventive, detective, and corrective controls mapped to NIST AI RMF outcomes and the GenAI Profile
- 2) What credible evidence demonstrates those controls are implemented and effective
- 3) How to tailor controls and evidence for generative AI risks such as hallucinations, jailbreaks, data leakage, and misuse

The NIST AI RMF organizes trustworthy AI practices across Govern, Map, Measure, and Manage. While the RMF is outcome-based (not a prescriptive control catalog), organizations implement controls to achieve those outcomes and produce evidence to demonstrate they work. The GenAI Profile specializes those outcomes for generative AI, highlighting risks like harmful content, prompt injection, jailbreaks, hallucinations, intellectual property and privacy leakage, provenance of synthetic media, and misuse at scale.

Control design begins by mapping risks and desired outcomes to specific control objectives. Examples by function:
- Govern: policies, roles/RACI, model inventory, procurement/supplier clauses, documentation standards (model/data cards), accountability and training.
- Map: intended use and misuse scenarios, stakeholder impact analysis, risk appetite/tolerance, context and data lineage, legal/ethical constraints.
- Measure: evaluation suites and test plans (safety, robustness, privacy, bias), red teaming, coverage criteria, reproducibility, and acceptance thresholds.
- Manage: risk treatment plans, guardrails (content filters, tool permissioning), human-in-the-loop review, incident response, rollback/kill switches, change management, and monitoring.

GenAI control patterns:
- Preventive: access control and rate limiting; safety policies embedded in prompts; system prompt hardening; retrieval filtering; PII and IP blocklists; constrained decoding; watermarking/provenance labeling for media; content policy enforcement.
- Detective: comprehensive logging of prompts/outputs/tool calls; abuse/anomaly detection; jailbreak/prompt-injection monitors; drift and regression dashboards; shadow/canary deployments; user reporting channels.
- Corrective: automatic output blocking/quarantining; takedown workflows; rapid model/config rollback; patching/fine-tuning; incident postmortems and control updates.

Evidence must be sufficient, appropriate, current, and linked to control objectives and RMF outcomes. Strong evidence is objective, reproducible, and versioned. Typical artifacts include: policies/SOPs and training records; RACI and governance minutes; model and data cards; data lineage and license attestations; evaluation plans, test datasets, and results with pass/fail thresholds; red-team reports with methodology and remediation tracking; guardrail and filter configurations; versioned system prompts and templates; monitoring dashboards and KRIs; incident tickets and postmortems; change logs and deployment approvals; third-party assessments and supplier attestations. For GenAI, add hallucination and harmful-content benchmarks, jailbreak and prompt-injection test results, privacy leakage canaries, and provenance/watermark implementation proofs (e.g., C2PA signing and verification logs).

• Control mapping: Tie each control to a specific AI RMF outcome and GenAI risk.
• Control types: Preventive, detective, and corrective layers reduce residual risk.
• Evidence quality: Versioned, reproducible, linked to acceptance criteria and retained per policy.

• Map layered controls to AI RMF outcomes and GenAI-specific risks.
• Produce versioned, reproducible evidence tied to acceptance criteria and remediation.
• Prioritize preventive, then detective and corrective controls, validated by rigorous evaluation and red teaming.
Congratulations! You have completed this lesson. You can now design RMF-aligned controls for GenAI systems and assemble credible evidence to demonstrate effectiveness.

title.en: Continuous Risk Management (NIST AI RMF & GenAI Profile)

body.en: In this lesson you will learn: 1) How to operationalize continuous risk management across Govern, Map, Measure, and Manage 2) How to monitor GenAI-specific risks with metrics, thresholds, and triggers 3) How to run change, incident, and improvement cycles with evidence updates

Risk in AI systems changes with data, models, users, and adversaries. The AI RMF emphasizes iteration: continually reassess context (Map), update measurements (Measure), and implement responses (Manage) under clear governance (Govern). For GenAI, continuous management must track misuse patterns (jailbreaks, prompt injection), model regressions (toxicity, hallucinations), privacy leakage, distributional shifts, and supply chain updates (new model releases, API behavior changes).

Key practices:
- Define KRIs and acceptance thresholds tied to RMF outcomes (e.g., harmful-content rate, hallucination rate on canonical tasks, refusal precision/recall, jailbreak success rate, PII leakage indicators, provenance adoption rate). Instrument telemetry and dashboards.
- Establish triggers and gates: pre-release evaluation gates; canary/shadowing; automatic rollback/kill switch when thresholds breach; incident severities and on-call runbooks.
- Run a risk register with owners, mitigations, and residual risk rationales; review regularly with cross-functional governance (legal, security, privacy, product, and domain experts).
- Maintain evaluation pipelines and data: update red-team corpora, injection/jailbreak test sets, and safety metrics as attackers evolve; validate reproducibility and coverage.
- Manage changes: version models/prompts/tools; document diffs and expected risk deltas; require approvals; update user docs and model/data cards.
- Learn from operations: analyze incidents and near-misses; implement corrective/preventive actions; recalibrate thresholds and controls; refresh training.
- External watch: track standards, regulations, supplier/model updates, and threat intelligence; adjust controls and evidence accordingly.

• KRIs and thresholds: Quantify risk and define objective triggers.
• Monitoring and telemetry: Capture prompts, outputs, tool calls, and guardrail outcomes with privacy-aware logging.
• Change and incident management: Gates, runbooks, rollback, postmortems, and continuous improvement.

• Continuous risk management requires defined KRIs, thresholds, and automated triggers tied to RMF outcomes.
• Maintain evaluation pipelines, red teaming, and change/incident management to adapt to evolving GenAI risks.
• Update governance artifacts and evidence with every significant change, incident, or shift in context.
Congratulations! You have completed this lesson. You can now implement continuous, RMF-aligned risk management for generative AI systems.
